task.goal: Make decisions from a weekly volunteer committee meeting turn into completed actions without making the chair a permanent bottleneck.
hard_constraints: Eight volunteers meet for 45 minutes; no paid project software.
Actions need owners and due dates but members can decline tasks.
Compare completion, rework and volunteer burden over one month.
task.available_resources: Shared notes and a basic calendar.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Consent-based action queue with explicit acceptance
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
The mechanism is a pull system: a committee decision becomes an active commitment only when a volunteer explicitly accepts a bounded task. This prevents apparent agreement from being mistaken for willingness to do the work.

Reserve the last eight minutes of each 45-minute meeting for action acceptance. In shared notes, record each decision’s intended result, smallest useful deliverable, completion criterion and proposed deadline. Invite volunteers to claim tasks; each may decline or negotiate scope and date. Every accepted action receives one owner and a due date. Unclaimed work stays visibly uncommitted, and the committee chooses to defer it, reduce it or abandon it. Nobody receives a task through silence.

Owners add their own calendar reminders and update their rows before the next meeting: completed with evidence, blocked with a specific request, or renegotiation needed. Allow only one active action per person initially. A rotating recorder maintains the queue during the meeting; the chair does not chase updates. Changes affecting the agreed result return to the committee, while owners control execution details.

This needs a shared-note template, calendar access and willingness to leave some decisions unimplemented. It is strongest when unclear commitments and overcommitment cause missed work. It may fail when nobody has capacity or necessary expertise; visibility cannot create either.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: For one month, alternate this method and the committee’s usual assignment method across comparable, low-risk actions. Both require willing owners and due dates. Freeze each action’s original deadline and completion criterion for measurement. Record completion by that deadline, substantive corrections or reopening within seven days, and weekly minutes spent on administration and chasing by each volunteer, including the chair. Report unclaimed work separately so selective acceptance cannot inflate success. Inspect results after four meetings, allowing seven days to observe late rework. The mechanism is challenged if accepted actions perform no better, unclaimed work accumulates, or administration merely shifts from the chair to everyone else. Small samples make findings provisional.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Rotating action steward with limited coordination authority
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
The mechanism is distributed coordination: a different consenting volunteer temporarily holds responsibility for follow-through, supported by explicit authority to resolve routine obstacles. This makes coordination an ordinary committee role rather than an implicit permanent duty of the chair.

During each 45-minute meeting, reserve five minutes to appoint the next week’s steward and review outstanding actions. The steward captures each accepted action in shared notes with its owner, due date, deliverable and completion criterion. Members can decline both tasks and the steward role. An action without an accepting owner remains uncommitted.

Before the meeting ends, identify foreseeable dependencies and authorize a narrow response to each: for example, obtaining an answer from another member or arranging a short discussion. The steward sends one consolidated calendar reminder and offers one brief unblock check during the week. They cannot assign unwilling people, change policy or silently extend deadlines. If an owner withdraws, the steward asks for a replacement or marks the action paused. At the next meeting, the outgoing steward hands unresolved items to the incoming steward through the same notes.

The change in outcome comes from supplying a named coordination function while preventing that function from attaching permanently to one person. It requires several members willing to rotate, access to the shared calendar and clear authority boundaries. It suits work blocked by dependencies more than work blocked by lack of time. Rotation can itself introduce lost context or inconsistent follow-up.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Over one month, split comparable accepted actions between rotating-steward support and owner-managed follow-through using the same notes template. Agree on the allocation before outcomes are known. Record original-deadline completion, corrections or reopened work within seven days, and each volunteer’s minutes spent executing, coordinating and attending meetings. Count the steward’s handoff time and the chair’s remaining interventions explicitly. Inspect handoffs after each meeting and compare results after four weeks, with seven additional days for rework observation. Reject or simplify the mechanism if coordination time increases without better completion, handoffs repeatedly lose information, or the chair still resolves most obstacles. A small trial cannot establish long-term willingness to rotate.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Protected execution time inside the weekly meeting
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
The mechanism is to replace some discussion with immediate execution. Instead of relying entirely on volunteers finding additional time later, the committee uses part of its existing shared time to finish small actions or produce inspectable first steps.

Structure the 45 minutes as five minutes reviewing prior actions, twenty minutes making decisions, fifteen minutes doing selected work and five minutes recording outcomes. For each decision selected for execution, define a useful deliverable that fits the work period: draft an announcement, prepare a purchasing list or complete an application section. One volunteer explicitly accepts ownership and a due date, which can be the meeting’s end. Others may help or decline; declining does not create a later obligation. Members without a suitable action can review shared materials or finish their participation early.

Use shared notes as the work surface and record links or text showing what was produced. Where work continues afterward, retain one consenting owner, a due date and a clear remaining step, with a calendar reminder. Reviewers check completed outputs against the agreed criterion during the next meeting. Facilitation and note-taking rotate among willing members, so the chair need not organize separate work sessions or chase everyone.

This requires actions that can be divided into meaningful short units and a committee willing to reduce discussion time. It could work because starting costs, clarification and access to colleagues are handled while everyone is present. It is less suitable for confidential work, physical errands or tasks awaiting outside responses. The main risk is displacing necessary decisions.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: For four weeks, alternate protected-execution meetings with the usual 45-minute format. Track all decisions and resulting accepted actions, including complex work that cannot fit a sprint. Compare original-deadline completion, substantive corrections within seven days, and total meeting, execution and coordination minutes per volunteer. Also record agenda items deferred because discussion time ran out. Inspect actual outputs rather than counting work started as work completed. Allow seven days after the final meeting to observe rework. The approach is challenged if it produces only trivial completions, defers important decisions, or fails to reduce outside-meeting burden. Differences between weekly agendas will limit causal confidence.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Bounded authority to finish without further approval
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
The mechanism is to remove repeat approval as a cause of stalled work. When the committee makes a decision, it also gives the accepting owner enough authority to complete it within explicit boundaries. The chair stops being the default approver for execution details.

Use six minutes of each 45-minute meeting to finalize action mandates in shared notes. Each mandate states the intended result, one consenting owner, a due date, observable completion criteria, permitted discretion and any limits on expenditure or external commitments. Members may decline or negotiate the task. Work without an accepting owner remains uncommitted. For example, an owner could publish a routine notice using agreed facts and a specified audience without returning for approval of every sentence.

An owner may act within the mandate and mark completion with evidence in the notes. Only a boundary-crossing change requires another committee decision; record that question for the next meeting rather than routing ordinary choices through the chair. Legally required approvals and existing financial controls remain applicable. Owners set their own calendar reminders, and a consenting recorder captures mandates during the meeting.

This requires trust, sufficiently clear decisions and tasks for which the committee can delegate execution authority. It could improve completion when volunteers wait for reassurance or repeated sign-off. It cannot solve insufficient capacity, and vague boundaries could increase rework. Its suitability is uncertain until the committee checks whether approval delays actually occur.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: For four weeks, allocate comparable, low-risk accepted actions between bounded mandates and the committee’s usual approval process. Both groups have willing owners, due dates and completion criteria. Record completion by the original deadline, approval-related waiting days, substantive corrections or reopening observed during the month, and each volunteer’s execution and administration minutes, including the chair’s. Count mandate-writing time within meeting burden. Compare actions with equal observation time and flag late-month actions whose rework remains unobserved. The mechanism is challenged if approval waiting falls without better completion, corrections rise, or drafting boundaries consumes more volunteer time than it saves. A small trial provides directional evidence only.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Book the work when accepting the action
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
The mechanism is to convert a general intention into a specific appointment with the work. An accepted action gets both a delivery deadline and an owner-chosen execution slot, reducing reliance on remembering the task and finding spare time later.

Reserve six minutes within each 45-minute meeting for action planning. Record each action’s deliverable, completion criterion, consenting owner and due date in shared notes. Members may decline. Before accepting, the prospective owner identifies a realistic calendar slot before the deadline and a concrete first step: for example, Wednesday at 19:00, open the venue list and request availability from three venues. The owner puts the appointment in their basic calendar; shared notes need only show that a slot exists, not disclose private calendar details.

If the work needs several sessions, the owner books enough time for the estimated effort or reduces the promised scope before accepting. They identify one predictable obstacle and a fallback, such as a second slot if childcare disrupts the first. If a slot is missed, the owner reschedules before the deadline or marks the commitment at risk in the notes. The committee handles unresolved risks during its next scheduled review; the chair does not maintain a separate reminder service.

This needs calendar access, reasonably predictable availability and tasks whose effort can be estimated roughly. It could work when willingness exists but intentions repeatedly lose out to competing demands. It offers little help with missing expertise or external dependencies. Calendar entries are planning aids, not evidence of progress, and volunteers must remain free to decline rather than invent unrealistic availability.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Over one month, allocate comparable accepted actions between calendar booking and a simple owner-plus-deadline list. Keep completion criteria and review time equivalent. Record original-deadline completion, substantive rework observed during the month, and weekly execution, planning and chasing minutes for every volunteer. Record missed appointments and rescheduling time without collecting private calendar details. Compare rework only across equal observation windows and identify actions still too recent to assess. The mechanism is challenged if appointments are routinely missed, completion does not improve, or scheduling burden outweighs reduced chasing. Inspect actual deliverables; a booked or attended slot does not count as completion.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Consenting backup pairs for continuity when availability changes
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
The mechanism is continuity through a prearranged backup: an action can survive its owner's unexpected loss of availability without waiting for the chair to find a replacement. This could help when volunteers intend to deliver but personal commitments disrupt execution.

Reserve seven minutes of the existing 45-minute meeting to arrange coverage for selected actions. In shared notes, record the deliverable, completion criterion, accepting owner, due date and a consenting backup. Either person may decline. The backup accepts a specific, limited rescue contribution, such as finishing a draft from existing notes, rather than an unlimited obligation to complete whatever remains.

At an agreed checkpoint before the deadline, the owner records completed work and whether help is needed. If the owner requests a handoff, or misses the checkpoint, the backup checks the notes and confirms whether they can take ownership. Transfer is explicit; silence never creates an obligation. If neither person has capacity, mark the action at risk for committee review. A short progress note makes transfer possible without the chair reconstructing events. Calendar reminders go to the pair.

This needs overlapping skills, some spare capacity and work that can be handed over safely. Begin with at most one backup commitment per member. Confidential or specialist actions may be unsuitable. The main uncertainty is whether backup coverage supplies useful resilience or merely reserves scarce volunteer time twice.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: For one month, allocate comparable, transferable actions between backup coverage and a simple consenting-owner-plus-deadline list. Use the same completion criteria. Compare completion by original deadlines, substantive corrections within seven days of delivery, and each volunteer's weekly execution and coordination minutes, including backup preparation and chair intervention. Inspect late-month deliveries only for the rework window actually observed. Record whether handoffs occurred and succeeded. Coverage is challenged if disrupted actions still stall, or any completion benefit requires disproportionate standby and handoff effort. If no availability disruptions occur, the trial cannot meaningfully test the proposed mechanism.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Recipient verification before an action is counted complete
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
The mechanism is a direct feedback loop between the person producing an output and the person who will use it. Completion means the output is usable for its agreed purpose, reducing work that appears finished in meeting notes but later needs correction or another chair-mediated discussion.

Within six minutes of each 45-minute meeting, record each selected action's consenting owner, due date and intended recipient in shared notes. The recipient may be another committee member who needs the result for a subsequent step. Both roles are voluntary. Together they write one observable acceptance check: for example, a venue comparison includes availability, total cost and accessibility information sufficient to choose a venue.

The owner posts the output directly in the notes. The recipient checks it by an agreed review deadline and either confirms acceptance or identifies the specific unmet criterion. The owner handles corrections directly with the recipient. New preferences beyond the agreed criterion become a separate committee request rather than silently expanding the task. Silence leaves the output marked 'delivered, awaiting verification'; it does not imply acceptance. The chair has no routine sign-off role.

This requires an identifiable user of the output, reviewers with relevant knowledge and willingness to give brief feedback. Use it only where usability can be checked cheaply. It could reduce ambiguous completion and downstream rework, but it adds review effort and can create a new bottleneck if recipients lack capacity. Shared notes and calendar reminders are sufficient.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Over one month, allocate comparable actions between recipient verification and owner-declared completion, with willing owners, due dates and written criteria in both groups. Compare usable outputs delivered by the original deadline, substantive correction cycles, and each volunteer's execution, review and coordination minutes. At the next meeting, briefly inspect outputs from both groups against their criteria so self-declared completion does not automatically score better. Count this inspection burden. Track review delays and chair interventions separately. Compare rework within equal seven-day windows and flag incomplete observation. The mechanism is challenged if verification delays completion without reducing unusable outputs or later corrections. Small numbers and reviewers influencing both groups limit confidence.

EXPAND.title: Standing mandates for recurring decisions
EXPAND.proposal:
The mechanism is to replace repeated committee approvals with bounded authority held by consenting volunteers. Routine work can proceed without waiting for the chair or another meeting, while consequential choices remain with the committee.

In one 45-minute meeting, spend ten minutes identifying two recurring activities that frequently wait for approval, such as publishing an already agreed announcement or arranging a routine event. In shared notes, define each mandate’s permitted decisions, limits, completion standard and conditions requiring committee discussion. Spending authority exists only within an explicitly approved budget. A volunteer may decline the mandate or negotiate its scope.

Each mandate holder records concrete actions with an owner and due date; a mandate itself does not count as an action. The holder may execute accepted work independently but cannot assign obligations to other volunteers. Calendar reminders support delivery. Members inspect outcomes during a five-minute weekly review rather than requiring the chair to approve each intermediate step. A holder can relinquish the mandate, leaving subsequent work visibly uncommitted until someone accepts it.

This could improve completion when approval delays, rather than insufficient effort, are the main obstacle. It needs repeatable work, clear boundaries and enough trust to tolerate differences in execution. It offers little benefit for novel or disputed decisions. Poor boundaries could increase rework or concentrate responsibility in a different permanent bottleneck; therefore mandates expire after the month unless their holders and the committee choose to renew them.
EXPAND.experiment: For one month, compare two similar recurring work streams: one uses a standing mandate and one retains committee approval. Both require consenting owners, due dates and explicit completion criteria. Record completion against original deadlines, time waiting for approval, substantive corrections within seven days of delivery, and each volunteer’s execution and coordination minutes, including the chair’s. Count mandate setup time and record eligible work left unclaimed. Inspect the underlying outputs at month end, allowing seven further days for late rework. The mechanism is challenged if approval waits fall but completion does not improve, boundary disputes increase, or the mandate holder’s burden becomes unacceptable. Differences between work streams make the result provisional.

EXPAND.title: Readiness gates before execution commitments
EXPAND.proposal:
The mechanism is to prevent avoidable stalls by separating a decision to pursue an outcome from permission to begin execution. An action enters execution only when its critical inputs and dependencies are available.

Use a small readiness checklist in shared notes: intended output is clear; necessary information or access exists; any required prior approval is obtained; and dependencies have confirmed availability. Discuss these questions when recording a decision, using no more than seven minutes of the 45-minute meeting for the combined action review. A missing prerequisite becomes a separate, bounded preparation action with a consenting owner and due date. The downstream work remains visibly waiting, without implying that someone has accepted it.

Once prerequisites are ready, a volunteer explicitly accepts the execution action and its due date. Anyone can decline preparation or execution work. Owners record evidence of readiness and completion directly in the notes and use the calendar for their reminders. They resolve ordinary execution details themselves; only changes to the agreed result require committee discussion. The chair does not certify every gate: the accepting owner checks the recorded evidence, with questions raised in the shared notes.

This could work when volunteers lose time starting work without information, access or reliable dependencies. It requires honest identification of prerequisites and preparation tasks small enough to complete. It cannot supply missing expertise or force an outside party to respond. Excessive checking could delay simple work, so routine actions with all inputs present pass immediately. Preparation progress must remain distinguishable from delivery of the committee’s intended result.
EXPAND.experiment: During four weeks, allocate comparable decisions to readiness gating or ordinary direct commitment, using a coin toss where practical. Both conditions use willing owners, due dates and completion criteria. Track decision-to-delivery time as well as original-deadline completion so later execution starts cannot manufacture success. Record blocked days, substantive rework within seven days, and each volunteer’s execution and administration minutes. Include waiting and unclaimed decisions in the comparison. A falsifying observation is that gated work spends as long blocked, delivers no sooner, and consumes more administration. Inspect a few stalled actions to see whether the checklist identified the actual missing input. Allow seven days after the month for rework observation; small numbers limit confidence.

EXPAND.title: Peer acceptance checks at the first consequential step
EXPAND.proposal:
The mechanism is early error detection: a consenting peer checks a small, representative output before the owner invests in the full action. This aims to reduce rework caused by different interpretations of a meeting decision without routing approval through the chair.

For actions where a wrong interpretation would be costly, record the intended result, completion criterion, owner and due date in shared notes. Invite a second volunteer to accept a narrowly defined check, such as reviewing the first paragraph of an announcement or the proposed event requirements. Both roles are voluntary. The reviewer receives a separate due date early enough to leave execution time and checks only the agreed criterion, rather than introducing personal preferences.

Reserve up to six minutes of each 45-minute meeting to identify actions needing a check and resolve disputed criteria. Owners and reviewers coordinate through the notes and calendar. A reviewer can decline; the owner then chooses whether to proceed within existing authority, seek another willing reviewer or return the action for rescoping. Work requiring formal approval cannot bypass it. If feedback would change the committee’s intended outcome, the committee decides; otherwise the owner incorporates it independently.

This could improve completion by catching misunderstandings while correction is cheap. It needs outputs that can be sampled early and reviewers with relevant knowledge and capacity. It is unnecessary for straightforward tasks and can become a new bottleneck if checks expand or reviewers respond late. Cap the expected check at five minutes and record missed checks rather than relying on the chair to chase them.
EXPAND.experiment: Over one month, compare similar accepted actions with and without an early peer check. Both groups retain the same final completion criteria, willing ownership and due dates. Record on-time completion, substantive changes caught early, corrections required after delivery within seven days, and execution, review and coordination minutes for every volunteer. Include time waiting for reviewers and the chair’s interventions. Inspect actual outputs rather than treating reviewer approval as proof of quality. The mechanism is challenged if late rework remains unchanged, deadlines slip while waiting for checks, or total burden exceeds the effort saved. Allow a seven-day observation tail after the month. Any apparent benefit remains uncertain with a small, uneven task sample.

EXPAND.title: Pre-agreed fallback paths for actions at risk
EXPAND.proposal:
The mechanism is to decide acceptable fallback behavior while making the original decision. When a predictable obstacle occurs, the owner can deliver a smaller useful result or stop futile work without waiting for the chair to arbitrate.

For suitable actions, record a preferred deliverable, a minimum useful fallback and an observable trigger in shared notes. For example: if a venue has not confirmed by Tuesday, use the already approved online format. Specify the owner, original due date and completion criteria for both outcomes. The volunteer explicitly accepts this bounded responsibility and may decline or negotiate it. A fallback cannot create obligations for another member without that member’s consent.

Spend up to seven minutes of the weekly 45-minute meeting defining fallback paths for actions with a foreseeable obstacle. Put the trigger date and delivery date in the basic calendar. The owner records whether the trigger occurred and which path was taken. Choices outside the approved paths return to the committee; choices inside them need no chair approval. Where no useful fallback exists, record that fact rather than inventing a weaker result merely to claim completion.

This could improve useful delivery when uncertainty repeatedly causes last-minute escalation or indecision. It requires obstacles that can be anticipated and fallback results the committee actually values. It does not solve a general lack of volunteer capacity. It may encourage premature retreat to easier work, so triggers must be observable and fallback delivery must be reported separately from full delivery. Defining elaborate contingencies for every action would impose more work than it saves.
EXPAND.experiment: For one month, compare similar uncertainty-exposed actions with pre-agreed fallbacks against actions using ordinary escalation. Both require consenting owners, original due dates and completion criteria. Record full delivery, fallback delivery and non-delivery separately; never combine them into an undifferentiated completion rate. Track post-delivery corrections within seven days and each volunteer’s execution, contingency-planning and coordination minutes, including chair interventions. Inspect triggered fallbacks to verify that their conditions occurred and their outputs were useful. The mechanism is challenged if it merely relabels failure, reduces full delivery without useful substitutes, or adds planning burden without reducing delays. Allow seven days after the month for rework inspection. Task differences and the number of actual obstacles will limit the comparison.

EXPAND.title: Preference matching before volunteers commit
EXPAND.proposal:
The mechanism is to improve the fit between tasks and volunteers before requesting commitments. An open call can leave suitable people silent while the same quick responders repeatedly accept work. A brief preference round exposes otherwise hidden willingness, relevant skills and constraints; the committee then proposes assignments that members can accept or decline.

Reserve eight minutes within each 45-minute meeting. Record a small batch of actionable decisions in shared notes, each with a concrete deliverable, completion criterion, estimated effort and proposed due date. All eight members simultaneously mark each task “interested,” “could help,” or “unavailable,” adding any relevant constraint. A blank response means unavailable, never consent.

A willing rotating facilitator proposes matches, starting with tasks that have the fewest suitable volunteers and favoring interested members whose current workload permits them. Members explicitly accept the scope and due date or decline without explanation. Resolve competing preferences briefly; leave unmatched work visibly uncommitted. The facilitator has no authority to assign tasks or chase delivery. Accepted owners update their own entries and calendar reminders, and execute within the recorded decision’s boundaries.

The outcome changes through better allocation, rather than stronger reminders: volunteers may finish more readily when work suits their interests, skills and availability. Simultaneous responses also reduce reliance on whoever speaks first. Implementation needs only a small table in the existing notes and a few members willing to facilitate the matching round.

This assumes that some tasks have multiple possible owners and that preferences reveal useful differences. It cannot create capacity or replace scarce expertise. Public preferences may still reflect social pressure, and matching can become burdensome if too many tasks are considered. Limit the round to the current actionable batch and record allocation time as volunteer burden.
EXPAND.experiment:
For one month, compare preference matching with a simple open call for owners. Where a meeting produces at least two reasonably comparable, independent actions, allocate them between methods by coin toss before asking for volunteers. Both methods use identical deliverable definitions, explicit acceptance, due dates and owner-managed reminders. If too few comparable actions arise, report a descriptive pilot rather than a causal result.

Track actions offered, accepted and completed by their original due dates; report unclaimed actions separately so selective acceptance cannot inflate success. Record corrections required to meet the original criterion and approximate rework minutes. Each member records weekly minutes spent on delivery, allocation, reminders and coordination, including the chair. Inspect how unevenly work is distributed.

The smallest early check is whether the first matching round reveals willing, suitable owners who would not have volunteered in the open call; ask that question briefly after allocation. After four weeks, improved completion with similar or lower rework and acceptable burden would support further use. No improvement in matches or completion, alongside extra allocation time, would count against the mechanism. Small samples and differences between tasks will leave substantial uncertainty.
